title: SQL: locking, deadlocks and optimistic vs pessimistic control
seriesDescription: Joins, aggregates, window functions and CTEs, indexes and EXPLAIN, ACID and isolation, locking. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.
description: Row locks, SELECT FOR UPDATE, NOWAIT and SKIP LOCKED job queues, deadlocks and how to avoid them, and choosing between optimistic (version column) and pessimistic locking. Checked on PostgreSQL 16.
source: PostgreSQL 16 documentation (explicit locking, SELECT locking clause, deadlock_timeout, lock_timeout); Designing Data-Intensive Applications ch. 7

questions.prompt: Match each PostgreSQL locking feature to its behaviour.

right.text: Takes an exclusive row lock; other writers and lockers wait
Takes a shared row lock; blocks writers but allows other shared lockers
Raises an error (SQLSTATE 55P03) instead of waiting for a locked row
Silently skips rows that are currently locked by someone else
An application-defined lock on a number, not tied to any row
Locks the whole table in ACCESS EXCLUSIVE mode

questions.explanation: FOR UPDATE locks stay until the transaction ends. NOWAIT and SKIP LOCKED are modifiers that change what happens when a row is already locked. Advisory locks are cooperative: nothing in the schema enforces them.

questions.prompt: Transaction T1 locks row A and then requests row B; transaction T2 locks row B and then requests row A. When PostgreSQL detects this deadlock, how many of the two transactions does it abort?
questions.explanation: The detector picks one participant (the one that ran the check) and aborts it with 40P01 deadlock_detected; the survivor continues once the victim releases its locks. The victim should be retried by the application.

questions.prompt: A jobs table has 10 rows with status 'queued' (ids 1 to 10). Worker A holds FOR UPDATE row locks on ids 1, 2 and 3 in an open transaction. Worker B runs SELECT id FROM jobs WHERE status = 'queued' ORDER BY id LIMIT 10 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED. How many rows does B get?
questions.explanation: B skips the three locked rows and locks ids 4 to 10, so 7 rows come back without waiting. (Verified on PostgreSQL.) Without SKIP LOCKED B would block on id 1; with NOWAIT it would fail with 55P03.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: A read-modify-write cycle that starts with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE cannot lose an update to another writer of that row.
questions.reason: FOR UPDATE takes a row lock that other writers and lockers must wait for until the transaction ends.

whys.a: Correct: the lock serialises the writers, which is exactly why the lost update is prevented.
whys.b: R is the mechanism behind A, so it does explain it.
whys.c: R is true, so this option wrongly calls it false.
whys.d: A is true, so this option wrongly calls it false.

questions.explanation: The price is blocking: keep the locking transaction short and never hold it across user think time or remote calls.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: Optimistic locking is the better default when write conflicts on the same row are rare.
questions.reason: Optimistic locking holds a database row lock for the whole time a user edits the form.

whys.a: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
whys.b: R is false, so this option wrongly calls both statements true.
whys.c: Correct: A is true; R is false because optimistic locking holds no lock, it only checks a version at write time.
whys.d: A is true, so this option wrongly calls it false.

questions.explanation: Optimistic = detect at commit (version column), cheap when conflicts are rare, wasteful retries when they are frequent. Pessimistic = lock up front, predictable when contention is high.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: Acquiring locks in the same order in every transaction prevents deadlocks between them.
questions.reason: PostgreSQL detects deadlocks automatically after deadlock_timeout and aborts one participant.

whys.a: Detection is the recovery mechanism; it does not explain why consistent ordering avoids the cycle.
whys.b: Correct: both are true, but a deadlock needs a cycle in the wait-for graph and consistent ordering makes a cycle impossible.
whys.c: R is true, so this option wrongly calls it false.
whys.d: A is true, so this option wrongly calls it false.

questions.explanation: Practical rule: update rows in primary-key order (ORDER BY id ... FOR UPDATE), and lock parent before child tables in every code path.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: While one transaction holds SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on a row, a plain SELECT of that row by another transaction waits.
questions.reason: FOR UPDATE conflicts with other FOR UPDATE locks and with UPDATE and DELETE on the same row.

whys.a: A is false, so both-true options are wrong.
whys.b: A is false, so both-true options are wrong.
whys.c: R is true, so this option wrongly calls it false.
whys.d: Correct: under MVCC a plain SELECT takes no row lock and reads the last committed version without waiting; R is true.

questions.explanation: Only other lockers and writers wait. That is why a read replica or a plain read never blocks behind a hot row lock.

questions.text: A deadlock is reported with SQLSTATE {1}. A statement that must fail immediately instead of waiting for a locked row uses {2}. To avoid deadlocks, take locks in a consistent {3}. PostgreSQL starts deadlock detection after {4} by default.
questions.explanation: deadlock_timeout defaults to one second: the check is only started when a lock wait lasts that long. lock_timeout and statement_timeout are separate safety nets.

questions.prompt: Table jobs(id, status, payload, created_at). Write the single statement a worker runs to claim the oldest 'queued' job so that concurrent workers never block each other and never take the same row.

checks.label: locks with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED

questions.model:
SELECT id, payload FROM jobs
WHERE status = 'queued'
ORDER BY created_at
LIMIT 1
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;
questions.explanation: Run it in a transaction, mark the row 'running' (or delete it) and commit. Verified on PostgreSQL: with another session holding the oldest row, the query returned the next one immediately. This is the standard database-as-queue pattern.

questions.prompt: Inside a transaction on accounts(id, balance), write the statement that reads the balance of account 1 and locks that row so concurrent transactions cannot change it until this transaction ends.
questions.model: SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE;
questions.explanation: FOR NO KEY UPDATE is a weaker lock that does not block foreign-key checks from child inserts and is enough when you do not change key columns. Object-mapping libraries expose the same thing as a pessimistic write lock mode.

questions.prompt: Table accounts(id, balance, version) is updated with optimistic locking. Write the UPDATE that sets balance to :new_balance for id :id only if the row still has version :version, and increments the version.

checks.label: checks the expected version in WHERE

questions.explanation: If the driver reports 0 affected rows, someone else won; raise a conflict and let the caller re-read and retry. This is exactly the statement that the version-column feature of an object mapper generates.

questions.prompt: Hundreds of checkouts per second decrement the stock of one hot product row. Which approach is best?

options.text: One atomic UPDATE ... SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE id = ? AND qty > 0, then check the row count.
options.why: Right: the row lock is held only for one statement and no retry loop is needed.

options.text: Read the stock, check it in application code and save with an @Version column, retrying on conflict.
options.why: Under heavy contention most attempts fail and retries thrash the row.

options.text: Run all checkouts at SERIALIZABLE and let the database sort it out, with no retry logic.
options.why: Many transactions would abort with 40001, and without retries those become errors.

options.text: SELECT the stock, check it in application code, then UPDATE it without any lock, since MVCC makes this safe.
options.why: MVCC does not stop two transactions reading the same quantity; stock goes negative.

questions.explanation: For hot rows prefer a single conditional statement over a read-then-write cycle. For counters at extreme rates, shard the counter across rows or use a queue.

questions.prompt: Select all situations that can cause a deadlock or long lock waits in PostgreSQL.

options.text: Two transactions update the same two rows in opposite order.
A transaction keeps row locks while it calls a slow external HTTP service.
options.why: Right: everyone queueing on those rows waits for the network call.

options.text: Two transactions run SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on overlapping row sets but with different ORDER BY clauses.
options.why: Right: different lock acquisition orders can form a cycle.

options.text: Many transactions run plain SELECTs on the same row at the same time.
options.why: Plain MVCC reads take no row locks and do not wait.

options.text: Two transactions insert into different tables and touch no common rows.
options.why: With no shared locks there is nothing to wait for.

questions.explanation: Fixes: consistent lock ordering, short transactions, lock_timeout, and retry on 40P01.

questions.prompt: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED gives every worker a consistent view of the whole queue.

options.why: The documentation says the opposite: skipping rows produces an inconsistent view of the data.
Right: it deliberately skips locked rows, so it is suitable for queue-like tables but not for general-purpose reads.

questions.explanation: That inconsistent view is the point: each worker sees only the rows nobody else has claimed. Do not use it for reports or aggregates.

questions.prompt: A row lock taken by SELECT ... FOR UPDATE in PostgreSQL stays held until the surrounding transaction ends, even after the SELECT statement itself has finished.

options.why: Correct: row locks last until commit or rollback (or until a savepoint taken before the lock is rolled back), not until the statement ends.
Wrong: the lock is not released at statement end, which is the misconception this option encodes.

questions.explanation: This is why a locking read must sit inside an explicit transaction: in autocommit mode the lock vanishes at once and protects nothing. Keep the transaction short.
